clue.text: Heats up, after slip welcomes end of Phil Salt

indicators.note: A slip is a lapse, and letters that have slipped are no longer standing where they were put.
To welcome someone is to take them in, so the extra letter joins the shuffled batch instead of sitting outside it.
The end of a name is its final character, so only the last letter of the word after it is wanted.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
the closing letter of Phil

explanation.walkthrough: Phil Salt opens the batting for England, so the two words read as one cricketer's name while the clue wants the surname on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A sulphate is a salt of sulphuric acid — the chemist's sense of salt, not the stuff in the cellar.

clue.text: Time that is left for King Charles?

blocks.note: a span of time is a stretch of it
i.e. is Latin id est, 'that is'
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.walkthrough: Three tiny conventions laid end to end, dressed up as a question about the monarch — and the question mark is there because the definition names one breed by its royal owner.
explanation.definitionFit: The King Charles spaniel is named after Charles II, who kept them, so the royal name defines the breed by example.

clue.text: Steals fifty-one paper planes, ultimately

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so the word beside it hands over its final letter alone.

blocks.note: L is fifty and I is one in Roman numerals
the Financial Times, Britain's business daily, is the FT
the last letter of planes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a theft of stationery, and 'paper' is the crossword's favourite newspaper rather than a sheet of the stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift something is to steal it — the informal sense behind shoplifting — and both are third-person verbs.

clue.text: Passionate about entertaining American city

indicators.note: You entertain guests by having them inside the house, so what follows is taken in by the letters before it.

blocks.note: someone hot on a subject is passionate about it
US is the everyday short form of the United States

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' sits next to 'Passionate' looking like a turning instruction; it belongs to the phrase instead, and the phrase is what supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Houston is the biggest city in Texas, so the bare word defines it by example — one place standing for the class.

clue.text: Try following beat music

indicators.note: What follows arrives afterwards, so the piece named first in the clue ends up second in the column.

blocks.note: to tan somebody is to give them a beating
a go is a try, an attempt at something

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' is where the surface wants you to hear rhythm, and the wordplay wants the thrashing sense of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tango is a dance and the music written for it, so 'music' defines it by example.

clue.text: One wearing confused tramp's sweater?

indicators.note: You wear a garment by getting inside it, so the single letter goes among the others rather than beside them.
Something confused has been put into disarray, so the letters will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
I is the Roman numeral one, worn inside the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweater' promises a jumper to go with the tramp's clothes, and the question mark is the setter admitting it means something that sweats.
explanation.definitionFit: An armpit sweats more than anywhere else on the body, so 'sweater' is a thing that sweats rather than a woollen top.

clue.text: At first, Rotherham United got better

indicators.note: At first points to the start of a word, so only the opening letter of the name is taken.

blocks.note: the initial letter of the Yorkshire town
nations that are united are allied

explanation.walkthrough: Rotherham United is a South Yorkshire football club, so the two words read as one team name — and the clue pulls them apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A patient or a side that rallied got better, recovering ground after a bad spell, and both are past-tense verbs.

clue.text: Star writer supported by Ravel

indicators.note: A support sits underneath what it holds, and in a down entry underneath means later in the column.

blocks.note: a pen does the writing, so it stands in for the writer
to ravel is to tangle — the capital letter is borrowed for the surface

explanation.walkthrough: Maurice Ravel is planted there to make you hunt for a composer. The lower-case verb 'ravel' means to tangle, which is where English gets 'unravel'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentangle is the five-pointed star drawn in a single unbroken line, so 'Star' names the shape directly.

clue.text: The Spanish probing 4 fruit

indicators.note: A probe goes into whatever it is examining, so these two letters push into the middle of the other word.

blocks.note: the answer to 4 down, borrowed whole
'the' in Spanish is el

explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference: solve 4 down first, then split it open. The name of this citrus is a squash of its two parents, tangerine and pomelo.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangelo is a citrus hybrid of tangerine and pomelo, so 'fruit' defines it by class.

clue.text: Broadcast about foreign cash settled matter

indicators.note: One thing placed about another goes round it, so the longer word splits and the coin drops into the gap.

blocks.note: a programme that was broadcast was sent out
the dime is the American ten-cent coin, foreign currency from a British desk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is a three-way trap — it can signal an anagram, or scattered seed, or, as here, plain past-tense 'sent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sediment is the matter that has settled out of a liquid, so the definition is literal once 'settled' is read as a verb.

clue.text: Plenty of waste exposed in American church

indicators.note: To expose something is to strip off what covers it.

blocks.note: A stands for American, as in the A of USA
EFFLUENT is liquid waste, here without its first and last letters
CE is the Church of England, the crossword's standard church

explanation.walkthrough: Wealth and sewage are one letter apart in English, and this clue makes you build the pleasant word out of the unpleasant one.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluence is plenty — a plentiful supply of money — and both words are mass nouns, so the swap is clean.

clue.text: Russian leader in square originally leading revolutionary

indicators.note: Originally means at the outset, so the word beside it gives up its opening letter only.
A revolution takes a thing all the way round, so the assembled letters are read from the far end back.

blocks.note: nine is a square number, three times three
the first letter of leading

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' earns its keep twice over: it is the instruction to read the letters backwards, and it describes the man the definition points at.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenin led the Bolsheviks and then the new Soviet state, so 'Russian leader' names him by the job he held.

clue.text: Perhaps Ant ignoring Conservative figure in the corner?

indicators.note: Perhaps flags an example rather than a synonym: the creature named is one member of the class, and the class word is what is wanted.
To ignore something is to leave it out, so the party's letter is dropped from the longer word.

blocks.note: an ant is one example of the class of small six-legged creatures
C is the standard abbreviation for the Conservative party

explanation.walkthrough: Ant of Ant & Dec, the British television double act, is what the surface is really about — a presenter snubbing a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is the small map or picture set into a corner of a larger one, so the definition describes its literal job.

clue.text: Produce social security cheque sent back in haste regularly by Earl

indicators.note: Sent back means returned the way it came, and along an across entry that direction is right to left.
Regularly asks for letters at a fixed interval, here every second one, so half of the word is dropped.

blocks.note: a giro was the benefit cheque the British state paid out through its Girobank, written here the other way round
the word taken as itself
the second and fourth letters of hAsTe
E is the abbreviation for earl in lists of the peerage

explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces in a row is a lot of joinery, and the giro is the one worth knowing: for decades 'the giro' simply meant the dole.
explanation.definitionFit: To originate something is to produce it, to bring it into being, and both are transitive verbs in the same form.

clue.text: Swimmer in Moselle on mobile!

indicators.note: Something mobile is free to move about, so the letters will not stay where the clue lays them.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells a phone call from a river valley, and 'on' looks like part of that sentence rather than part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemon sole is a flatfish, so 'Swimmer' defines it by what it does — the crossword's usual nudge towards a fish.

clue.text: Friend drinking sparkling wine beginning to crave champ

indicators.note: A drinker takes the liquid inside.
The beginning of a word is its first letter, so only that one character of the verb is used.

blocks.note: a mate is a friend
Asti is the sparkling white wine of Piedmont
the opening letter of crave

explanation.walkthrough: 'Champ' looks like the winner standing beside the wine that is being poured; it is the verb, to chew noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: To champ is to chew hard and noisily, which is the everyday word for what the answer says in Latin.

clue.text: Cancel patent on receptacle

indicators.note: In a down entry one thing rests on another by standing above it, so the first word tops the second.

blocks.note: a patent lie is an overt one, out in the open
an urn is a receptacle for ashes or for tea

explanation.walkthrough: 'Patent' looks like the document you file at the office; here it is the adjective meaning obvious, which is stressed on a different syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: To overturn a verdict is to cancel it, the courtroom sense, and both words are transitive verbs.

clue.text: Quietly hiding, Silvanus perhaps turned to leave

definitions.note: The answer is an adverb that survives only in the phrase 'lie doggo', so the definition describes the state rather than swapping in word for word.

indicators.note: Perhaps marks an example: the Roman named is one of a class, and it is the class word that supplies the letters.
A thing turned round is read the other way, so those three letters arrive in reverse.

blocks.note: Silvanus was the Roman god of woods and fields, and GOD is turned round here
to leave is to go

explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter points hard at a person, and the wordplay only wants his job description — a deity, turned about.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie doggo is to stay hidden and keep quiet, the way a dog lies still, which is exactly what the definition describes.

clue.text: Actor's school subjects, in brief

indicators.note: In brief asks for short forms, so each subject arrives as the abbreviation a timetable would print.

blocks.note: PE is physical education on a school timetable
SCI is the timetable short form of science

explanation.walkthrough: One plural phrase covers two subjects, and the surname is assembled from them without a single letter to spare.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Pesci is an American film actor, so the bare word 'Actor' defines the surname by example.

clue.text: Priest likely to be flexible

blocks.note: P is the dictionary abbreviation for priest
liable to happen means likely to happen

explanation.walkthrough: 'Liable' overlaps with 'likely' in only one sense — liable to rain, likely to rain — and that is the sense the wordplay leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pliable bends without breaking, which is flexible in its literal sense; of a person it means easily talked round.

clue.text: Be left at home with husband with tax going up

indicators.note: In a down entry the letters can be read from the bottom upwards, so this word is written climbing.

blocks.note: somebody at home is in
H is the abbreviation for husband, as on a family tree
to tax someone is to tire them, and TIRE is set climbing

explanation.walkthrough: Inheritance tax is sitting in plain sight in the surface, which is what makes the seam between definition and wordplay so hard to find.
explanation.definitionFit: To inherit is to be left something in a will — the definition states the same act from the other side.

clue.text: Outgoing person is greener?

blocks.note: the -er ending is the comparative, asking for more, and more of a thing is extra
vert is green in heraldry and in French

explanation.walkthrough: One word of wordplay carries both pieces, and they come out in the opposite order to the way English says them. The -a- spelling is the psychologist's.
explanation.definitionFit: An extravert turns outward for stimulation — sociable, talkative, energised by company — which is what 'outgoing person' describes.

clue.text: Prayer from setter in hole

indicators.note: A thing said to be in another sits within it, so the shorter word lands in the middle of the longer one.

blocks.note: an opening in the body, wanted here as a plain hole
gel is the stuff that sets — hair gel — so the word for what sets is used loosely for the setting agent

explanation.walkthrough: In a cryptic, 'setter' almost always means the person who wrote the clue, so it takes some resisting to read it as a substance instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Angelus is the Catholic devotion recited at morning, noon and evening to the sound of a bell, so 'Prayer' names it by class.

clue.text: Satellite rattles around

indicators.note: To rattle around is to knock about loose, so the letters are shaken out of the order they came in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: Telstar relayed the first live television pictures across the Atlantic in 1962, and the surface makes it sound like loose change in a drawer.
explanation.definitionFit: Telstar was a communications satellite, so the class word defines it by example — one craft standing for the type.

clue.text: Cook rises with traditional dish

indicators.note: Cooking mixes the ingredients together, so the letters go into the pot and come out in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: Bread rising beside a cook makes a smooth kitchen sentence, and that is what hides 'with' — it is fodder, not the little word joining two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish stew is the national dish of mutton, potatoes and onion, so the phrase defines it by class.

clue.text: More sage in group of women's English recipe

blocks.note: the Women's Institute, the British countrywomen's organisation, is the WI, and the possessive adds the S
E is the abbreviation for English
R is the old prescription and cookery abbreviation for recipe

explanation.walkthrough: Sage is a herb as well as an adjective, which is the only reason a recipe and some English cooking are in the surface at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage means wise, so 'More sage' is its comparative — and the answer is a comparative too, which keeps the swap exact.

clue.text: Good public transport system is the ultimate aim

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
the rail network is a country's public transport system

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole phrase at the end, and the surface spends its words on trains so that you read 'ultimate aim' as part of the sentence about them.
explanation.definitionFit: The grail is the object of an endless quest, the figurative sense used whenever something is called a holy grail.

clue.text: Ace boss is winning

blocks.note: the ace is the A of a suit of cards
the head of a firm is its boss

explanation.walkthrough: Two short words that read as praise for a person — an ace boss — and neither is doing anything but handing over letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A side that is ahead is winning at that moment, the running-score sense rather than an outright victory.

clue.text: Former leader, second-class, getting money from Iran returned

blocks.note: a second-class mark is a B
the rial is the Iranian currency, written backwards here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Former leader' would fit hundreds of names, so the wordplay has to settle which one — and the surface's talk of Iranian money is the setter making that look like news.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Blair led the Labour party and was Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007, so the phrase defines the surname by example.

clue.text: Right to enter exam? It's tough

indicators.note: To enter is to go inside, so the legal term is placed within the other word rather than added after it.

blocks.note: a resit is the exam taken again after a failure
a lien is the legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' is R in most cryptics, and the whole clue depends on it not being R here — it is the four-letter legal one instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone resilient is tough: they take knocks and spring back, so the adjective swaps straight in.

clue.text: Happenings in flat extremely tedious

indicators.note: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so both outer letters are kept and everything between them goes.

blocks.note: a flat surface is an even one
the first and last letters of tedious

explanation.walkthrough: 'In flat extremely tedious' reads as a grumble about a dull apartment, which hides both the adjective meaning level and the instruction beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Events are things that happen, so the plural noun answers the plural definition exactly.

clue.text: Campaigner is more vulgar about essay on the radio

indicators.note: One word set about another wraps round it, so the sounded letters end up in the middle.
On the radio you hear a word without ever seeing it written, so it is the sound that counts and not the spelling.

blocks.note: crude means vulgar, and the comparative adds the -r
a short piece of writing is an essay, and saying those two letter names aloud is saying the word

explanation.walkthrough: The letter-name homophone is worth collecting: 'essay', 'excel' and 'empty' are all just letters read aloud, and setters use them for short awkward chunks.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusader campaigns hard for a cause — the figurative sense taken from the medieval holy wars — so the noun swaps in directly.
